claims.evidence: Source read. OWASP Cheat Sheet Series (Session Management, JSON Web Token, Authentication, Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention, Multifactor Authentication) read from a shallow clone at commit ae965343cb82e6b8f42aff1ccee57c4fa0f171c2, which was also searched for QR-login material; OWASP QRLJacking page (OWASP/www-community commit ce2814653f497a7a9ebadce39ce7f84bb3c603e4, also the QRLJacking README at defd5e3ebf6de72356bcc5cea476760c00273193 and its wiki at 25b457e41efcc9493d0266646bd48848a6dd3dc1) and the MDN cookies guide (commit 19370346042efad9e179fbf1f55deeeadee98c40) read; segno 1.6.6 source and the PyJWT usage page read. A toy QR login (Python 3.13.16 standard library, segno 1.6.6, PyJWT 2.14.0) was run on localhost on 2026-10-18; its numbers are one run on the authoring machine. RFCs and protocol specifications were not reachable and were not read; no real QR-login service was examined; OWASP's mitigations were not tested.

claims.claim_vi: The source lists six ways to manage identity at login: Session (server stores identity, browser gets a session ID cookie; 'cookies don't work well across devices'), Token (identity encoded in a token; 'no server session storage; but tokens need encryption/decryption'), JWT (standard identity tokens with digital signatures, no server session), SSO (central authentication service), OAuth2 ('limited access to your data on one site by another site, without giving away passwords') and QR code (a random token in a QR code; scanning logs you in without typing a password).
claims.verified_by: Source body read.

claims.claim_vi: A session works by the server answering a sign-in with a cookie that holds a session ID, which the browser sends back and the server checks; the browser stores cookies and sends them back to the same server.
claims.verified_by: Read from a clone of the repository at the pinned commit (the introduction and the basic sign-in example of the cookies guide). That a random token has the same state model as a session (the server looks the value up) is the author's general knowledge and the content of lesson sd-14-010.

claims.claim_vi: A signed JWT carries its data and a signature, and the verifier needs only the key: the payload could be read without any key and verification with another key or after editing the payload (role changed to admin) raised InvalidSignatureError; a random token holds nothing to decrypt and is checked by look-up.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP states that JWTs are used for the ID token of the identity layer on top of OAuth and that an OAuth 2 access token can be a JWT; that signed JWT gives authenticity and a JWT can also be encrypted for confidentiality; that a signed JWT is not confidential because its payload is only base64url encoded.
claims.verified_by: Read from a shallow clone of the repository at the pinned commit.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP states that JWT is often suggested for stateless user sessions but this is frowned upon, that such sessions need a way to invalidate them, for example a deny list, and that with a deny list sessions are no longer completely stateless.
claims.section: Considerations about using JWTs, Not using JWTs

claims.claim_vi: OWASP states that OAuth is an authorization framework for delegated access to APIs, that OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of OAuth, and to use OpenID Connect for authentication and SSO and OAuth for authorization; so OAuth2 is not a way to recognise the user by itself.

claims.claim_vi: SSO as one central login service that holds the login session while the applications receive the authentication result is the author's general knowledge; OWASP's QRLJacking page describes SSO as one account that lets a user authenticate to multiple services.
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge for the 'central service holds the session' wording; the QRLJacking page was read at the pinned commit for the one-account description; not checked against a protocol specification.

claims.claim_vi: A miniature QR login worked in four steps: the browser asked for a one-time random token (the server recorded it as pending), the browser polled, a phone with its own logged-in session posted the token, and the next poll gave the browser a new session while the token became used. Before the confirmation the poll only answered pending and the browser had no session.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by executing the experiment script qr_login_exp.py (Python 3.13.16 standard library toy server on a random localhost port, segno 1.6.6, PyJWT 2.14.0) on the authoring machine on 2026-10-18; the script and its output are in the session scratchpad, not in the repository. Sections 2 of the output. The polling is the toy server's choice; real services may differ (not examined).

claims.claim_vi: The OWASP QRLJacking page describes the QR login model as a user scanning a QR code generated by the service with a client app on a trusted device such as a smartphone, which transmits the code to an identity provider that validates it.
claims.verified_by: Read at the pinned commit (the 'Login With QR codes, a feature or a bug?' part).

claims.claim_vi: With segno 1.6.6 a 30-character payload (a prefix plus the 22-character token) made a version 2 QR code of 25 x 25 modules without border at error level L, byte mode; two different tokens gave the same size.

claims.claim_vi: Expiry (toy server, 1 second set for the test): a confirmation after the time got 410 expired; a token confirmed in time but polled after the time also got 410 and the browser had no session (a choice of the toy). The OWASP QRLJacking page says a well implemented QR login process should have an expiration interval for the QR codes.

claims.claim_vi: Confirmation by the wrong phone (toy server, assuming the attacker knows the token shown on the victim's browser; how is not tested): the attacker's phone confirmed the victim browser's token and the victim browser then was logged in as the attacker; in the mirror case the victim's phone confirmed a token shown on the attacker's browser and the attacker's browser was logged in as the victim. The server logged both confirms in the same form (phone user, token prefix, address, user agent); all addresses were 127.0.0.1, so the run cannot show whether address checks would help.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP's QRLJacking page names the mirror case QRLJacking (the victim scans the attacker's QR code, which results in session hijacking), says the top recommendation is to stop using Login with QR code except when necessary, and lists four mitigations: session confirmation (a confirmation message or notification showing characteristic information about the session), IP restrictions, location-based restrictions and sound-based authentication. It also quotes a patent abstract of a design in which the QR code encodes a server address and the mobile device sends a device ID.

claims.claim_vi: OWASP's CSRF cheat sheet describes login CSRF (the attacker makes the victim's browser authenticate as the attacker's own account; the victim then enters card details there) and says it can be mitigated by pre-sessions (sessions before authentication) with tokens in the login form, or custom request headers in AJAX requests. It is written for login forms, not QR login, and was not tested against the QR flow.

claims.claim_vi: Each device has its own session: with the same user logged in on two clients, the two session values differed, a client with no cookie got 401, and logging out on one client left the other logged in. A token kept in an app also lives on one device, so the source's 'cookies don't work well across devices' is not a difference between cookie and token.

design_notes_vi: Hai khung thẻ (nhớ người đã đăng nhập, nhờ bên khác làm chứng) trả lời hai câu hỏi cho mỗi cách, một khung trình tự cho đăng nhập bằng mã QR và một khung ghi nhớ hai điều về mã QR. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source says cookies don't work well across devices; the lesson shows each device logs in and holds its own session, and that a token kept in an app is also per device, so this is not a cookie-versus-token difference.
The source says tokens need no server session storage; the lesson says that holds only for self-contained tokens such as a signed JWT, while a random token is looked up on the server.

The source says tokens need encryption/decryption; the lesson says a random token needs look-up only, a signed JWT needs signing and verifying and its payload is readable without a key, and encryption is a separate option (JWE).
The source says a JWT needs no server session; the lesson adds OWASP's caveat that invalidating a session needs a deny list, after which it is no longer stateless.
The source lists OAuth2 among the ways to manage identity at login; the lesson says OAuth is delegated authorization and recognising the user needs an authentication layer on top of it.

The source says scanning the QR code logs you in; the lesson adds that the phone must already be logged in and confirms the token with its own session while the browser waits and then receives a new session.
The source says the QR code encodes a random token; the lesson says that is one design, and the OWASP page quotes another in which the QR code holds a server address and the phone sends a device ID.

The source does not mention that the server cannot tell whether the phone's owner meant to log in the browser showing the code; the lesson shows this in both directions (attacker's phone, attacker's QR code) and reports what OWASP says about it.
